title: Waterproofing Roof Slabs, Terraces and Bathrooms Right from the Start
desc: Why roof slabs, terraces and bathrooms leak, the waterproofing layers needed, construction order, water testing for acceptance and common mistakes.
summary: The spots in a house most prone to leaks, waterproofing principles from the design stage, the construction order, and how to flood-test before tiling.
body: p

Leaks are the defect that costs homeowners the most money and stress after moving in: yellowed ceilings, peeling paint, rusting reinforcement in the concrete. Fixing a leak after tiling and ceiling installation often costs many times more than doing it right from the start. This article summarises the waterproofing principles for the three places where problems most often occur.
h2
1. Why do roof slabs, terraces and bathrooms leak?
ul
Roof slabs and terraces take direct sun and rain; concrete expands and contracts with day-night temperature, so it easily develops hairline cracks and water follows the cracks down to the ceiling.
Bathrooms are always damp and have many pipes passing through the slab; a single gap around a pipe collar lets water leak to the floor below.
Wall bases and junctions of slab to wall and slab to parapet are where the waterproofing layer is often missed or made without enough height.
A slab without enough fall towards the drain leaves water standing for long periods, which will find a way through.
h2
2. Waterproofing starts at the design stage
p

Waterproofing is not just brushing on a layer of material. The drawings need to show clearly: the slab fall to the drain, the position and number of drains, the bathroom floor level relative to the room floor, the detail of pipe collars through the slab, the wall base detail and the protective layer on the roof. For a house that must hire a design firm (a house of 3 or more floors, with a basement, with total floor area of 250 m² or more, or 12 m or higher - under Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP), you should require the drawing set to include a separate waterproofing detail sheet.
h2
3. The correct construction order
ol
Dense, solid slab concrete: pour continuously, compact well and cure moist for the proper time - this is the first waterproofing layer.
Treat weak points first: seal pipe collars through the slab with non-shrink mortar or special fittings; clean and level the surface and round the slab-to-wall corners.

Apply the waterproofing layer exactly as the manufacturer instructs (number of coats, waiting time between coats, mesh reinforcement at corners and pipe collars). The waterproofing layer must be carried up the wall base, not stop at the slab surface.
Flood test before the protective layer and tiling (section 4).
Protective layer, screed to falls, and tiling; on a roof, add a heat-insulating layer if the design calls for it.
p
Choose waterproofing materials of clear origin; for construction materials on the list requiring conformity certification, see construction materials that must have conformity certification.
h2
4. Water testing - an acceptance step not to be skipped
p

Once the waterproofing layer is dry, block the drains and flood the whole slab surface for the time set by the material's technical instructions and the design, then inspect the ceiling of the floor below, the wall bases and around the pipe collars. Only when there is no sign of dampness should work on the upper layers continue. It is advisable to record the water test result in the work acceptance record and keep photos; this is the basis for asking the contractor to repair if leaks appear later during the warranty period (see warranty for house construction).
h2
5. Common mistakes and how to avoid them
ul
Applying waterproofing to a dusty, wet or pitted surface - the material peels after a while.
Waterproofing only the slab surface and not carrying it up the wall base; water follows the mortar joints at the wall base to the next room.
Chasing the slab to install pipes after waterproofing without redoing the waterproofing.
Skipping the water test to keep to the schedule.
Finishing workers walking on or stacking materials on the layer and puncturing it before the protective layer is in place.
p

If your house is already leaking, you need to find the true source of the water before repairing - sometimes the water comes from a leaking supply or drain pipe rather than the slab.
